content: 1. Calcium channel blockers and isoniazid can interfere with blood glucose control in patients taking Metformin HCl. When these drugs are administered to a patient on Metformin, close monitoring for loss of blood glucose control is necessary. Similarly, when these drugs are withdrawn, the patient should be observed for hypoglycemia. 2. Pharmacokinetic studies in healthy volunteers have shown that the co-administration of Metformin with propranolol or ibuprofen does not alter the pharmacokinetics of either drug when given as a single dose. 3. Metformin has minimal binding to plasma proteins, making it less likely to interact with highly protein-bound drugs such as salicylates, sulfonamides, chloramphenicol, and probenecid, compared to sulfonylureas, which are extensively bound to serum proteins. 4. During pregnancy, abnormal blood glucose levels are strongly associated with an increased risk of congenital abnormalities. Most experts recommend using insulin during pregnancy to maintain blood glucose levels as close to normal as possible. 5. Animal reproduction studies are not always predictive of human response. Metformin HCl should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed, as there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. 6. Metformin was not found to be teratogenic in rats and rabbits at doses up to 600 mg/kg/day, which corresponds to approximately two to six times the maximum recommended human daily dose of 2000 mg based on body surface area comparisons. 7. 8. There is no specific guidance from the Australian Drug Evaluation Committee (ADEC) regarding the use of Metformin in pregnant women. 9. There is no FDA guidance on the use of Metformin during labor and delivery. 10. Studies in lactating rats indicate that Metformin is excreted into milk at levels comparable to those in plasma. However, similar studies have not been conducted in nursing mothers. 11. Due to the potential risk of hypoglycemia in nursing infants, a decision should be made to either discontinue nursing or discontinue the drug, considering the importance of the medication to the mother. If Metformin HCl is discontinued and diet alone is insufficient for blood glucose control, insulin therapy should be considered. 12. The safety and effectiveness of Metformin HCl for treating type 2 diabetes have been established in pediatric patients aged 10 to 16 years. However, studies have not been conducted in children under 10 years of age. 13. Evidence from well-controlled studies in adults, along with additional data from a controlled clinical study in pediatric patients aged 10 to 16 years, supports the use of Metformin HCl in this age group. The study demonstrated a similar glycemic control response to that seen in adults, with adverse effects comparable to those in adults. 14. The maximum recommended daily dose of Metformin HCl in pediatric patients is 2000 mg. 15. Controlled clinical studies of Metformin HCl in elderly patients did not include sufficient numbers to determine whether they respond differently from younger patients. However, other clinical experience has not identified differences in responses between elderly and younger patients. 16. Metformin is substantially excreted by the kidneys, and the risk of serious adverse reactions is higher in patients with impaired renal function. Therefore, Metformin HCl should only be used in patients with normal renal function. 17. Since aging is associated with reduced renal function, Metformin HCl should be used with caution in elderly patients. Dose selection should be based on careful and regular monitoring of renal function, and elderly patients should generally not be titrated to the maximum dose of Metformin HCl. 18. There is no FDA guidance on the use of Metformin with respect to specific gender or racial populations. 19. There is no FDA guidance on the use of Metformin in patients with renal or hepatic impairment. 20. There is no FDA guidance on the use of Metformin in women of reproductive potential or in immunocompromised patients. 21. There is no fixed dosage regimen for managing hyperglycemia in type 2 diabetes with Metformin HCl or any other pharmacologic agent. Dosage must be individualized based on effectiveness and tolerance, without exceeding the maximum recommended daily doses. 22. The maximum recommended daily dose of Metformin HCl is 2550 mg in adults and 2000 mg in pediatric patients aged 10 to 16 years. 23. Metformin HCl should be administered in divided doses with meals. It should be started at a low dose with gradual dose escalation to reduce gastrointestinal side effects and identify the minimum dose required for adequate glycemic control. 24. During treatment initiation and dose titration, fasting plasma glucose should be monitored to determine the therapeutic response and identify the minimum effective dose. 25. The therapeutic goal is to decrease fasting plasma glucose and glycosylated hemoglobin levels to normal or near-normal levels using the lowest effective dose of Metformin HCl, either as monotherapy or in combination with sulfonylurea or insulin. 26. Monitoring blood glucose and glycosylated hemoglobin levels will help detect primary failure (inadequate glucose lowering at the maximum recommended dose) and secondary failure (loss of glucose-lowering response after initial effectiveness). 27. Short-term administration of Metformin HCl may suffice during periods of transient loss of control in patients usually well-controlled on diet alone. 28. In adults, clinically significant responses are generally not observed at doses below 1500 mg per day. A lower starting dose with gradual increases is recommended to minimize gastrointestinal symptoms. 29. The usual starting dose of Metformin HCl is 500 mg twice daily or 850 mg once daily, given with meals. Dosage increases should be made in increments of 500 mg weekly or 850 mg every two weeks, up to a total of 2000 mg per day in divided doses. 30. Patients can also be titrated from 500 mg twice daily to 850 mg twice daily after two weeks. For those requiring additional glycemic control, Metformin HCl may be given up to a maximum daily dose of 2550 mg. 31. Doses above 2000 mg may be better tolerated when given three times a day with meals.
